title: The four watches of the night
hook: the four watches of the night as the stages of a life (Sri Rag M1, ang 74)

segments.voice: Yesterday, machhuli, the little fish in the river: the One was never far. Today Guru Nanak lays a whole life over a single night.

Before clocks, a night was measured in watches. Guards on a city wall, sailors on a ship, merchants camped by the road: the dark was split into four stretches of about three hours, and each had someone awake. You'd know the watch by how the night felt. The first, still warm from the day. The deep middle ones. The last, cold and gray-blue, just before dawn. Guru Nanak took those four watches and turned them into a map of a human life.
screen: `A NIGHT IN FOUR WATCHES.` → `GUARDS, SAILORS, CARAVANS.` → `A MAP OF A HUMAN LIFE.`

segments.voice: The hymn is called a pehre, from pahar, a watch. It's in Sri Rag, beginning on ang 74, and Guru Nanak addresses it to vanjaariaa mitraa: O my merchant friend. The listener is a trader on a journey, sent out with capital, expected to come back with something to show for it. In the first watch, the hymn says, by the Lord's command you came into the womb, and there you remembered the One. You came into the world naked, and naked you'll go. In the second watch you forgot. You were passed from arm to arm, adored, as Krishna was in Yashoda's house, and your mother said: this is my son. In the third watch your mind was fixed on wealth and on your own young body, and the Name didn't come to mind. In the fourth watch the reaper comes. Nobody knows the hour, and the merchant's accounts are read: what did you trade your life for? It's a sobering hymn, and Sikhs sing it as one. But it isn't meant to frighten. Notice who is speaking: a friend, mitraa, calling out to a traveler while there's still night left. Naming the watches means a person can wake up in any of them. A child can remember. A busy parent in the third watch can stop. Someone very old, in the cold last stretch before dawn, can still turn. The question isn't how far the night has gone. It's whether you're awake for the watch you're in.
screen: `PEHRE: A HYMN OF WATCHES.` · `O MY MERCHANT FRIEND.` · `WOMB, CHILDHOOD, WEALTH, THE REAPER.` · `WAKE UP IN ANY WATCH.` · then, large: `WHICH WATCH AM I IN?`

segments.voice: Sit with the four watches, beginnings, being carried and loved, building and earning, and the late cold watch for settling accounts, and ask honestly, without judging the answer: which watch am I in? Then ask the friend's question: what am I trading this watch for? If you pray, you can say Waheguru once and rest there.
Pahar, a watch, a quarter of the night: Guru Nanak's map of a life in four of them, womb, childhood, the busy middle, and the last watch, sung to a merchant friend while there's still time.
Your line: which watch am I in. Any watch is a good one to wake up in. Day six hundred fifty, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing Guru Nanak's Sri Rag pehre in kirtan, each stanza beginning with the watch of the night and addressing the listener as vanjaariaa mitraa, O merchant friend.

what a scholar hears: the pehre genre, begun by Guru Nanak and taken up by later Gurus in Sri Rag, uses the merchant (vanjaaraa) and the watches of the night to frame a life as a journey to be accounted for.
